A.R. Radcliffe-Brown. The British anthropologist who developed structural functionalism, a theoretical framework for analyzing how institutions, rituals, and kinship systems maintain social cohesion and structure.

Radcliffe-Brown pioneered the study of kinship systems as structural wholes. He demonstrated how marriage rules, descent, and obligation patterns organize entire societies. He developed structural functionalism, arguing that social institutions exist to maintain social integration and must be analyzed in relation to the whole social structure. This was a crucial theoretical move for the discipline.

He conducted extensive fieldwork among the Andaman Islanders, analyzing their rituals, kinship, and emotion-management practices in his monograph The Andaman Islanders, published in 1922. This fieldwork became foundational to his theoretical framework.

Radcliffe-Brown distinguished his structural functionalism from Malinowski's psychological functionalism. Where Malinowski emphasized how cultural institutions meet individual psychological needs, Radcliffe-Brown emphasized society's logical structure. The two were rivals in British anthropology, yet both foundational to it, debating functionalism against structuralism.

In 1937, Radcliffe-Brown founded the Department of Social Anthropology at Oxford University. From there, he trained a generation of influential British anthropologists including Max Gluckman and Meyer Fortes, who would dominate mid-twentieth-century anthropology.

He argued for a natural science of society, rejecting history and psychology as explanatory frameworks in favor of comparative structural analysis. This position shaped how anthropology would approach its subject matter for decades to come.
